title: Philemon

stories.title: 📜 Philemon
summaryBullets: Paul, a prisoner of Christ Jesus, and Timothy our brother, To Philemon our beloved fellow worker, (1:1).
to Apphia our sister, to Archippus our fellow soldier, and to the church that meets at your house: (1:2).
Grace and peace to you from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ. (1:3).
I always thank my God, remembering you in my prayers, (1:4).
because I hear about your faith in the Lord Jesus and your love for all the saints. (1:5).
I pray that your partnership in the faith may become effective as you fully acknowledge every good thing that is ours in Christ. (1:6).
I take great joy and encouragement in your love, because you, brother, have refreshed the hearts of the saints. (1:7).
So although in Christ I am bold enough to order you to do what is proper, (1:8).
I prefer to appeal on the basis of love. For I, Paul, am now aged, and a prisoner of Christ Jesus as well. (1:9).
I appeal to you for my child Onesimus, whose father I became while I was in chains. (1:10).
Formerly he was useless to you, but now he has become useful both to you and to me. (1:11).
I am sending back to you him who is my very heart. (1:12).
I would have liked to keep him with me, so that on your behalf he could minister to me in my chains for the gospel. (1:13).
But I did not want to do anything without your consent, so that your goodness will not be out of compulsion, but by your own free will. (1:14).
For perhaps this is why he was separated from you for a while, so that you might have him back for good — (1:15).
no longer as a slave, but better than a slave, as a beloved brother. He is especially beloved to me, but even more so to you, both in person and in the Lord. (1:16).
So if you consider me a partner, receive him as you would receive me. (1:17).
But if he has wronged you in any way or owes you anything, charge it to my account. (1:18).
I, Paul, write this with my own hand. I will repay it— not to mention that you owe me your very self. (1:19).
Yes, brother, let me have some benefit from you in the Lord. Refresh my heart in Christ. (1:20).
Confident of your obedience, I write to you, knowing that you will do even more than I ask. (1:21).
In the meantime, prepare a guest room for me, because I hope that through your prayers I will be restored to you. (1:22).
Epaphras, my fellow prisoner in Christ Jesus, sends you greetings, (1:23).
as do Mark, Aristarchus, Demas, and Luke, my fellow workers. (1:24).
The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit. (1:25).
crossRefs: Ephesians 1:15-16: Thanksgiving for faith and love.
2 Corinthians 7:13: Comfort and joy through others’ love.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: אָסִיר לַמָּשִׁיחַ (ʾāsîr la-māšîaḥ, sense), Greek: δέσμιος Χριστοῦ (désmios Christoû, NT), Aramaic: אסירא דמשיחא (ʾasirā d-mešiḥā)
translationNotes.note: Paul describes himself as imprisoned on account of his service to Christ.

The name means Useful, and it was a common slave name; owners named slaves for what they wanted out of them. Paul plays on it three times and English can only show one. In verse 11 he is achrestos, useless, and now euchrestos, useful. In verse 20, 'let me have some benefit from you', the verb is onaimen, built on the same root as the man's name. Paul is punning on a slave's name while asking his owner to take him back as a brother.

Under Roman law a slave who left remained his owner's property wherever he went, and the law was built to get him back. Owners advertised, and professional slave-catchers, fugitivarii, worked for a fee. A recovered runaway could be flogged, branded on the forehead, or fitted with an iron collar; collars survive with the message cast into them telling the finder to return the wearer to his master. Anyone who sheltered another man's slave was liable to the owner for the loss. Sending Onesimus back was the legally safe act; the letter he carried was not.

translationNotes.term: No longer as a slave, but a beloved brother
translationNotes.note: Rome had a formal route out of slavery: an owner could free a slave before a magistrate, by entering him on the census, or by will, and a slave freed that way by a Roman citizen became a citizen himself, still owing his former owner deference and set days of work as a patron. Paul does not name that procedure. He asks Philemon to receive Onesimus as he would receive Paul (verse 17), says he will do more than is asked (verse 21), and leaves it there. The letter is also addressed to Apphia, Archippus, and the assembly meeting in the house (verses 1-2), so the request was read out in front of everyone who would see the answer.

translationNotes.term: I write this with my own hand
translationNotes.original: Greek: τῇ ἐμῇ χειρί (tē emē cheiri)
translationNotes.note: Letters were normally dictated to a trained secretary, and the sender then wrote the last lines himself as a signature. The secretary of Romans names himself in the text: 'I, Tertius, who wrote down this letter' (Romans 16:22). Paul flags his own hand in 1 Corinthians 16:21, Galatians 6:11, Colossians 4:18, and calls it the mark in every letter in 2 Thessalonians 3:17. Here that hand signs a debt: charge whatever he owes to my account, I will repay it. It is written in the shape of a promissory note.

Xenia is both the guest quarters and the bond itself. Guest-friendship in that world was a formal, binding, reciprocal obligation, not a courtesy: the host owed a guest food, lodging, and protection, and the tie passed down to the children of both houses. In the Iliad two warriors find mid-fight that their grandfathers were guest-friends, and they refuse to fight each other and swap armour instead (Iliad 6.212-231). Paul asks for a room in the house of the man he is asking to take back a runaway.

stories.keyTakeaway: Paul greets Philemon and gives thanks for his love, faith, and the refreshment he has brought to the saints.

intro:
Philemon was written by Paul the apostle (Philemon 1:1), with Timothy named as co-greeter, during Paul's first Roman imprisonment of AD 60-62. It is the fourth and last of the "prison epistles" (along with Ephesians, Philippians, and Colossians), and Paul mentions his chains repeatedly in this short letter (Philemon 1:1, 9, 10, 13, 23, where he calls himself "a prisoner for Christ Jesus" and refers to Epaphras as "my fellow prisoner"). The letter is addressed primarily to Philemon, a wealthy believer in Colossae whose home was large enough to host the local church (Philemon 1:2: "to Philemon our beloved fellow worker and Apphia our sister and Archippus our fellow soldier, and the church in your house"); Apphia is traditionally identified as Philemon's wife and Archippus, who is also mentioned in Colossians 4:17, as their son or another member of the household. Philemon had likely been converted under Paul's three-year ministry in Ephesus (Acts 19, c. AD 53-56), as Philemon 1:19 implies that Philemon owed Paul his "very self," meaning his salvation. The letter was carried to Colossae by Tychicus, the same courier who delivered Ephesians and Colossians on the same journey (Colossians 4:7-9 names Tychicus as the bearer of Colossians, accompanied by Onesimus, "our faithful and beloved brother, who is one of you"). The occasion for the letter is an unusual one. Onesimus, a slave belonging to Philemon, had run away from his master in Colossae (and possibly stolen from him, per Philemon 1:18: "If he has wronged you at all, or owes you anything, charge that to my account"); he had made his way to Rome and somehow come into contact with Paul in his house arrest. Under Paul's ministry, Onesimus had become a believer (Philemon 1:10: "I appeal to you for my child, Onesimus, whose father I became in my imprisonment"). Now Paul is sending Onesimus back to Philemon with this letter, asking Philemon to receive Onesimus not merely as a slave returned but "more than a slave, as a beloved brother" (Philemon 1:16). Paul plays on the meaning of Onesimus's name (Greek onēsimos, meaning "useful" or "profitable"): "Formerly he was useless [Greek achrēstos] to you, but now he is useful [Greek euchrēstos] to you and to me" (Philemon 1:11). Paul writes this single verse of financial guarantee in his own handwriting: "I, Paul, write this with my own hand: I will repay it - to say nothing of your owing me even your own self" (Philemon 1:19). Returning a runaway slave to his master was legally hazardous for Onesimus (Roman law permitted owners to brand or kill runaways), and Paul's letter is a delicate personal appeal designed to ensure Onesimus's safe and dignified reception. According to early church tradition reported by Ignatius of Antioch (writing c. AD 107 in his Letter to the Ephesians 1:3), Onesimus later became the bishop of Ephesus, though whether the bishop is the same person as the runaway slave is not certain. Paul (originally Saul) was born in Tarsus of Cilicia around AD 5-10 to a Hebrew family of the tribe of Benjamin, educated in Jerusalem under Gamaliel the Pharisee before his conversion on the Damascus road and his apostolic ministry to the Gentiles; he was martyred by beheading in Rome under Nero around AD 66-67 (see the introduction to Romans for the full biographical sketch).

The historical setting is the Roman Empire in the early 60s AD, during Paul's house arrest in Rome and at the height of the Roman institution of chattel slavery. Slavery was ubiquitous in the Roman world: by some estimates between a quarter and a third of the population of the Italian peninsula was enslaved, and across the empire millions of human beings lived as the legal property of others. Roman slaves had no legal personhood; they could be bought, sold, beaten, tortured, sexually used, or killed by their owners at will (though some emperors limited the worst abuses). Runaway slaves (Latin fugitivi) were hunted by professional slave-catchers; on recapture they could be branded with the letter "F" (fugitivus) on the forehead, fitted with iron collars listing their owners' names, sent to the mines, or simply executed. Roman law required anyone who harbored a runaway slave to pay the owner damages and return the slave; concealing a fugitive could itself be a criminal offense. Paul's decision to send Onesimus back to Philemon (rather than keep him in Rome, as he might have liked, Philemon 1:13) was therefore an act of high risk for Onesimus; the letter functions both as a personal plea to Philemon and as Onesimus's safe-conduct pass. Colossae itself was the small Phrygian city in the Lycus Valley described in the introduction to Colossians, about a hundred miles east of Ephesus and one of three cities (with Laodicea and Hierapolis) clustered in the upper Lycus valley. The Roman emperor was Nero (AD 54-68), in the relatively benign early years of his reign before the great fire of Rome and the Christian persecution.

Philemon is the fifty-seventh book of the Christian Bible, the eighteenth book of the New Testament, and the last of Paul's thirteen letters in canonical order. At twenty-five verses (a single chapter in modern printings), it is the shortest of Paul's letters and one of the shortest books in the New Testament; only 2 John (13 verses) and 3 John (14 verses) are shorter. The earliest surviving manuscript is Papyrus 87 (P87, c. AD 200), a small fragment containing Philemon 1:13-15 and 24-25, the oldest known fragment of the letter; other early witnesses include Codex Sinaiticus (4th century) and Codex Alexandrinus (5th century AD). Philemon is the New Testament's only sustained example of Christian engagement with the institution of slavery: Paul does not stage a public abolition campaign or attack the legal system of slavery directly; instead he asks one slaveholder to receive one runaway slave back not as property but as a brother in Christ, and lets the implications of that recognition work their way through the moral imagination of the church. Within three centuries the Christian moral pressure begun in letters like Philemon would contribute to the gradual easing and legal reform of Roman slavery; within nineteen centuries the abolitionist movements of Britain and the United States would cite Philemon explicitly as the New Testament's foundational statement of the equality of all believers regardless of social status.
